title: Some umps fear ABS is causing fans to judge them by near-impossible standards
content:
Most businesses would balk at creating a system that subjects some of its employees to public embarrassment. But with its implementation of the Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) challenge system this season, Major League Baseball did just that to its umpires.

Some fans see the early results from ABS as proof umpires are incompetent. Some players and league officials say the opposite actually is true. But not all fans grasp the distinction between a call overturned by a tenth of an inch and one overturned by two inches. They just see that it was reversed, and draw their own negative conclusions.

Well, ABS is not perfect, either. I like it, as I wrote after the opening weekend. But I said then that it was the shiny new toy phase, the robots at their most romantic. In talking to some umps since, they’ve expressed reservations about the system.

The league said during spring training that the median margin of error on any given pitch in ABS is about one-sixth of an inch. That seems like a miniscule amount, but according to the website Tap to Challenge, 28 overturned calls through Monday –  an average of nearly three a day – fell within that margin.

Some umpires, speaking on condition of anonymity because both the league and their union wants them to refrain from public comment, are quietly stewing. They say fans are judging them by a near-impossible standard, and fear the game under ABS ultimately will suffer.

Those umpires expect pitchers and catchers eventually will grow angry that more balls are getting called in the smaller ABS zone, both by plate umps and the robots. The human zone was three-dimensional. The robot version is 2-D, hanging like a pane of glass across the middle of the plate. Many in the sport expected the redefined strike zone to increase the walk rate. So is it any coincidence that the combined 269 walks issued Saturday and Sunday were the most in any two-day span in the modern era?

Perhaps those two days were just a blip, a small-sample aberration in the first month of the season, when hitters generally swing the least. Perhaps pitchers and umpires are simply adjusting to the new technology, and by midsummer any early kinks will be forgotten. To this point, the complaints from pitchers have been minimal. And pitchers say at least some umps are fine with ABS, too.

“We’ve only really had one game where it’s been a lot – I think there were 11 challenges in the game,” said Kansas City Royals right-hander Seth Lugo, referring to a 13-9 Royals victory over the Minnesota Twins on April 1. “We were all thinking that the umpire (Andy Fletcher) was starting to get pissed off and someone asked him about it and he was like, ‘This is great. I’m getting better in-game, so this is cool.’”

Most fans, to this point, also think ABS is cool. The system not only holds plate umpires more accountable, but also introduces new layers of strategy, making games more entertaining. Oh, and let’s not forget: The umpires, in at least one sense, warrant only so much sympathy. They agreed to ABS in their latest collective-bargaining agreement, effectively letting the genie out of the bottle.

In exchange for their consent, the umps received concessions in other aspects of the deal, according to a person briefed on the details. The only condition in the agreement was that ABS must be approved by the joint competition committee, an 11-member group in which owners hold the majority and thus ultimate control. The umpires did not extract the same type of “call stands” provision that exists in instant replay for other calls on the field, where challenges can not be overturned without clear and convincing evidence.

The ABS equivalent would be a buffer zone allowing for calls within a specific margin of error to remain unchanged. Such a zone existed pre-robot world. The league, in its internal evaluations, did not penalize the umps for calling pitches a strike that missed the plate but hit the buffer zone.

ABS offers no such forgiveness. The league is steadfast about its accuracy. As The Athletic’s Jayson Stark wrote last month, league officials said MLB is 95 percent confident a pitch would be within 0.39 inches of the location where ABS pinpoints it. The league also said it is 99 percent confident the location would be within 0.48 inches of where the system said it landed.

That’s not perfection. With the league affording ABS a margin of error, the umpires are justified in asking for their own accommodation. But when they brought the matter to the joint competition committee, their concerns were dismissed, according to one person briefed on the discussions.

The league’s argument is that an ABS buffer zone would be impractical. Imagine, for example, a 3-2 pitch that is called a strike, shown to be a ball on the ABS scoreboard graphic, then ultimately ruled a strike because it was in the buffer zone. Such an outcome likely would leave fans confused and upset. ABS is far more clear-cut. And the league, after putting the umpires in a difficult spot, says they are performing exceedingly well.

“Major League umpires hold themselves to the highest standard and deeply care about getting calls right. We appreciate the professionalism of our umpires and their commitment to the good of the game and the wishes of fans,” Michael Hill, MLB’s senior vice president of on-field operations, said in a statement to The Athletic.

“As they adjust to the new zone, we commend the umpires for being the most accurate as a group in history, building off last season’s historic high with a 93.5 percent accuracy rate on pitches this year (through April 7), up 0.8 percent through the same number of games in 2025 (92.7 percent). We are also pleased that on the closest of pitches, those being challenged, umpires have been correct nearly half of the time (46.2 percent).”

Commissioner Rob Manfred, in his future public appearances, should drive home the point. The ABS data thus far shows just how precise the best umpires really are. The average miss of the 11 most accurate umps is 0.7 inches or less, according to Tap the Challenge. For the 40 most accurate, it’s one inch or less. Erich Bacchus currently is the worst, with an average miss of 2.28 inches. CB Bucknor, whose back-to-back missed strike three calls on the Cincinnati Reds’ Eugenio Suárez became a cause celebré on the opening weekend, is seventh worst, with an average miss of 1.36.

As in any profession, some umps are better than others. But those who want the league to abandon the challenge system and go full ABS should heed the words of Baltimore Orioles right-hander Chris Bassitt, who values the skill of the umpires.

“I don’t think people realize 0.2, 0.3 inches off the plate — they’re like, oh my gosh, I can’t believe you missed that call,” Baltimore Orioles right-hander Chris Bassitt said. “Go get a ruler out, please, and realize how much they just missed it by. He barely missed it.

“This guy is throwing 96 mph, and the ball moved 18 inches sideways. You have no idea what you’re talking about. You’ve never even seen this. So the fact these umpires are that good, let’s not take that away from them. These umpires are literally that good. I could not be more in favor of keeping umpires in this game.”

Over time, as the umpires grow more comfortable with the system, their accuracy should be even greater, particularly with the league taking steps to help them adjust.

Through their earpieces, umpires are for the first time getting in-game feedback on calls at their request. After games last season, they had the ability to compare their called pitches against the ABS zone in their computer system. And before games this season, they are receiving photos of each hitter on both clubs with lines drawn for the top of the zone (53.5 percent of the hitter’s height) and bottom (27 percent).

Still, some umpires worry. At every major-league park, the league employs a Ball-Out-Strike System (BOSS) operator who is responsible for ensuring the correct strike zone is used for each hitter – as opposed to say, the 5-foot-11 Trent Grisham getting stuck with the zone of the 6-7 Aaron Judge. Some of the BOSS operators, like some of the pitch-clock operators, are hourly employees.

Others are full-time. The umps wonder: Should hourly employees be holding the keys to the ABS kingdom?

Such questions are fair. MLB often is guilty of steamrolling change without giving proper deference to those affected – the third-base coaches who this season were ordered to stay inside their designated boxes, the front-office executives whose schedules the league jammed by moving the draft from June to July, just weeks before the trade deadline. But the umps have little choice but to adapt.

Detroit Tigers right-hander Casey Mize, one of four player representatives on the competition committee, said he recently had a conversation with Bill Miller, the one umpire representative, asking the 30-year veteran his thoughts on ABS.

“He has been in the league and hasn’t had any training with this and that’s a problem,” Mize said. “The younger umpires have. But the older guys haven’t. They’re kind of doing the best they can.

“Unfortunately, social media is probably going to blow him up for it. Not just him, I’m saying all of them. Being in the league as long as they have, this is literally brand new to them. They haven’t had a crash course on it outside of a few spring training games. But he said, overall, he thinks it’s a useful tool.”

Not all umpires agree with Miller. They’re understandably sensitive to the criticism ABS unleashed, considering their degree of difficulty in learning a new system and new strike zone in real time. None of the umps mind when ABS corrects their egregious misses. But when calls one-tenth of an inch off are lumped into the same “mistake” bucket as those bad errors, the credibility of the system suffers.

As with most rules changes, unintended consequences were inevitable. It’s bad enough when a good umpire is made to look foolish. It will be worse if pitchers start growing exasperated over losing strikes. And far worse if a postseason game is decided by an overturn that, due to the margin of error, might have been flat wrong.

-The Athletic’s Zack Meisel, Jayson Stark and Cody Stavenhagen contributed to this story
